data.Brute-Force:
- Recursive DFS with `sum` passed by reference (`void getSum(TreeNode* node, int &sum)`)
- Base case: `if(node == NULL) return;`
- Before recursing into `node->left`, check if it's a left leaf: `node->left != NULL && node->left->left == NULL && node->left->right == NULL`
  - If true: add `node->left->val` to `sum`, don't recurse further into it
  - If false: recurse normally via `getSum(node->left, sum)`
- Always recurse normally into `node->right` (no special check needed)
data.Optimal Approach: - Same as above — this is already optimal at O(N)/O(H), no further optimization possible (must visit every node once)
data.Gotcha-Point:
- A node being a "left leaf" is determined by which edge it's reached through (left child of parent), NOT by whether the parent lacks a right child
- Left-leaf check needs all 3 conditions together: `node->left != NULL`, `node->left->left == NULL`, `node->left->right == NULL` — missing any one breaks correctness
- Check must happen at the parent level (before recursing into the child), since a node doesn't inherently know if it's a left or right child once inside its own call frame
- Removing the `else` (recursing into `node->left` unconditionally even after adding it as a left leaf) causes redundant work but not double-counting — not a correctness bug, just wasted call frames
data.My Mistake:
- Initially thought "left leaf" = leaf whose parent has no right child — wrong; it's purely about which side the leaf itself is attached on
- Initially used only `node->left->left == NULL` to check leaf-ness — missed that `node->left->right` could still be non-NULL, incorrectly classifying single-right-child nodes as leaves

**Complexity:**
- Time: O(N) — visits each node once
- Space: O(H) — recursion stack, H = height of tree

data.Brute-Force:
- BFS (level-order) using `queue<pair<TreeNode*, TreeNode*>>` — stores (node, its parent)
- Start: `q.push({root, NULL})`
- For each level:
  - Save `levelSize = q.size()` **before** the loop (snapshot, since queue size changes as children are pushed)
  - Loop exactly `levelSize` times, dequeuing `{curr, par}`:
    - Guard before pushing children: `if(curr->left) q.push({curr->left, curr})`, same for right — avoids pushing/dereferencing NULL
    - If `curr->val == x` → `parentX = par` (NOT `curr` — must store the parent, not the node itself)
    - If `curr->val == y` → `parentY = par`
  - After the level's loop, check:
    - Both NULL → not found yet, continue to next level
    - Exactly one set → return `false` (safe because `x`/`y` each appear exactly once in the tree — if one isn't at this depth, they can never be cousins)
    - Both set → return `parentX != parentY`
data.Optimal Approach: - Same as above — already optimal, O(N) is the floor since you must potentially visit every node
data.Gotcha-Point:
- Must snapshot `levelSize = q.size()` before the loop — using `while(!q.empty())` directly would mix levels since children get pushed mid-loop
- Always guard `if(curr->left)` / `if(curr->right)` before pushing — pushing a NULL child crashes on `->val` access next iteration
- Store the **parent** (`par`), not the current node (`curr`), when a match is found — easy mix-up since both are in scope together via structured bindings
- Variables declared via `auto [curr, par] = ...` inside the `for` loop go out of scope after the loop ends — can't reference `par` outside it
- "Found at same level but different parents" is what makes them cousins — don't get the equality check backwards (`==` means NOT cousins, `!=` means cousins)
- Trailing `return true;` after the while loop is unreachable dead code, needed only to satisfy the compiler — reachable-code guarantee comes from problem's constraint that `x`, `y` always exist in the tree
data.My Mistake:
- Initially assigned `parentX = curr` instead of `parentX = par` — stored the matched node itself instead of its parent
- Initially forgot NULL guards before pushing children, causing a crash when dequeuing a NULL node and accessing `->val`
- Initially wrote the same-level-both-found comparison backwards/against wrong variable (`parentX == par && parentY == par`) instead of comparing `parentX` against `parentY`

**Complexity:**
- Time: O(N) — each node visited once
- Space: O(N) — queue can hold up to the widest level (technically N/2 for a complete tree's last level, but constants drop in Big-O)

data.Brute-Force:
- Treat every node as a potential "peak" of the path
- For each node, do a fresh DFS to compute best downward sum into left and right subtrees
- Combine as node.val + leftSum + rightSum, update global max
- O(N) work per node × N nodes = O(N²) time
data.Gotcha-Point: A node can return only one-directional extension to its parent, but can still contribute both directions to the global max at itself — these are two different computations reusing the same clamped sums.
data.My Mistake: Initialized global max to 0 instead of INT_MIN, causing failure on all-negative trees (path must contain at least one node, so 0 isn't a valid neutral value).
data.Optimal Approach:
- Single post-order DFS; each call returns "best downward sum starting at this node" to its parent
- Clamp negative child sums to 0 (don't extend into a branch that hurts the sum)
- At each node, update global max using node.val + leftSum + rightSum (allows the path to "bend" at this node)
- Return node.val + max(leftSum, rightSum) to parent (path can only extend one direction upward)
- O(N) time, O(H) space

data.Gotcha-Point: Sorting pair<int,int> directly sorts by first element then second automatically — no custom comparator needed since the tie-break rule (row then value) matches lexicographic order exactly.
data.My Mistake: Multiple syntax/logic bugs on first pass — missing null base case, used map::insert (no-op on existing key) instead of operator[]+push_back for appending, and initially tried to push vector<pair<int,int>> directly into vector<int> result without extracting values or using a reference binding in the range-for loop.
data.Optimal Approach:
- DFS from root, tracking (row, col): left child is (row+1, col-1), right child is (row+1, col+1)
- Group nodes as map<col, vector<pair<row, value>>> — map keeps columns sorted automatically
- For each column, sort its vector directly on (row, value) pairs — lexicographic sort handles row-then-value tie-break for free
- Extract just the values (in sorted order) into a vector<int> per column, assemble into final vector<vector<int>>
- O(N log N) time, O(N) space

data.Problem: Requirements needed to construct a unique BT
data.Gotcha-Point: Uniqueness fails specifically when a node has only one child — Preorder and Postorder become identical for left-child-only vs right-child-only cases, while Inorder distinguishes them by capturing relative position.
data.Optimal Approach:
- Recognize Inorder is the only traversal that captures left/right positional info relative to a root.
- Preorder or Postorder gives the root; Inorder is needed to split into left/right subtrees.
- (Pre, Post) fails because single-child cases produce identical Pre/Post sequences for different tree shapes.
- (X, X) fails because repeating the same traversal adds no new information.
- Rule: return true iff exactly one of the two traversal types is Inorder (2) and the other is Pre/Post (1 or 3); false if both same, or if the pair is (Pre, Post).
- O(1) time, O(1) space.
data.Brute-Force:
- No real "brute-force" here — this is a conceptual/lookup problem, not a search-space problem.
- The only naive approach would be to try reconstructing trees for both interpretations and check if they always match, which isn't practical to code directly.
data.My Mistake: Initially assumed Inorder alone was sufficient (defaulted to "middle element = root" without justification); needed a concrete counterexample (root=1, right-skewed) to see the ambiguity.

data.Optimal Approach:
- If the start or end cell is 1, return -1 immediately
- Use `dist[n][n]` initialised to -1, which doubles as the visited marker

- Return `dist[n-1][n-1]`, which is -1 if unreachable. O(N²) time, O(N²) space

data.Gotcha-Point: The path cost is the max edge, not the sum, so the relaxation becomes `max(dist[u], w)` instead of `dist[u] + w`. Dijkstra's greedy still holds because extending a path never lowers a max.
data.Optimal Approach:
- Treat each cell as a node, with 4-directional edges of weight |h[u] - h[v]|.
- Run Dijkstra with a min-heap keyed on effort, where `dist[r][c]` is the minimum possible max-edge to reach (r,c).
- Relaxation: `newEffort = max(dist[u], |h[v] - h[u]|)`. Update and push if `newEffort < dist[v]`.
- Skip stale heap entries, and return as soon as the destination is popped.
- O(N·M·log(N·M)) time, O(N·M) space.

data.Brute-Force:
- Enumerate every path from (0,0) to (n-1,m-1) with DFS/backtracking.
- Track the max absolute difference along each path and keep the minimum over all paths.
- Exponential time, since the number of paths in a grid blows up.

data.Gotcha-Point: `parent[]` is a per-node table of "who I came from", not a path. The route only appears when you hop along it from n back to the source, and the result list (not `parent[]`) is what you reverse.
data.Optimal Approach:
- Run Dijkstra with a min-heap from node 1, with `dist[]` initialised to INF and `parent[]` initialised to 0.
- On every strict improvement `dist[v] > dist[u] + w`, set `parent[v] = u` and push to the heap.
- If `dist[n]` is still INF, return `{-1}`.
- Else walk from n via `parent[]` until 0, `push_back` each node, then `push_back(dist[n])`, and reverse once.
- Optional early exit: break when n is first popped from the heap.
- O((V+E) log V) time, O(V+E) space
data.My Mistake: Used a single vector (then a map) to store the path instead of a per-node parent array; sized arrays `n` instead of `n+1` for 1-indexed nodes; scanned `parent[]` from the end instead of hopping along the links.

- Keep a visited set per path and compare the total weight at every arrival at n.

data.Gotcha-Point: A popped node's distance is final because every other route goes through a heap node with distance >= current, and non-negative weights can't make it shorter. Negative weights break this. Also, skip stale PQ entries (distance > dist[node]) to avoid reprocessing adjacency lists.
data.Optimal Approach:

- Min-heap of {distance, node}. Pop the smallest tentative distance, which is final
- Skip the entry if distance > dist[node] (stale entry)
- Relax each neighbour: if dist[node] + w < dist[nbr], update and push
- Return dist[]
- O((V+E) log V) ≈ O(E log V) time, O(V+E) space

data.Optimal Approach:
- Characters are nodes, and each "a comes before b" constraint is a directed edge.
- Compare only adjacent word pairs, since sortedness is transitive. The first differing character gives the edge s1[j] → s2[j]. Then break.
- If no mismatch is found and the first word is longer than the second (e.g. "abcd" before "abc"), the input is invalid, so return "".
- Run Kahn's algorithm (BFS topological sort) on all K nodes.
- If the topo order has fewer than K nodes, there is a cycle, so return "". Otherwise map the order back to characters.
- O(N·L + K) time, O(K + N) space.

data.Gotcha-Point: Don't clear `pathVisited` on unsafe nodes. Leaving them marked turns `pathVisited` into a permanent "unsafe" marker, so later DFS calls reaching them get the right answer and no separate result array is needed. Unmark only on the safe exit.
data.Optimal Approach:
- Use `visited` and `pathVisited` arrays. Run DFS from every unvisited node.
- A node is unsafe if it is on a cycle or can reach one. A terminal node is safe by default.
- In DFS, if a neighbour is unvisited, recurse. If it returns false, return false and leave this node marked in `pathVisited`.
- If a neighbour is visited and still marked in `pathVisited`, return false (cycle, or leads to an unsafe node).
- If all neighbours are safe, unmark the node in `pathVisited` and return true.
- Collect all nodes with `pathVisited == 0` in one pass for ascending order. O(V+E) time, O(V) space.

- Mark the node safe only if every path ends at a terminal node.
- No memory between runs, so shared sub-paths are re-explored for each starting node.
- O(V·(V+E)) time in the worst case.

data.Problem: Find the MST Weight (Kruskal) — Follow-up (MST Edges)
data.Optimal Approach:
- Flatten the adjacency list into edges (weight, u, v), keeping only `node < neighbour` to dedupe.
- Sort edges by weight ascending.
- Build a DSU over V vertices.
- For each edge, if the ultimate parents differ, record the edge in the MST and union by size.
- Break once the MST holds V-1 edges.
- O(E log E) time, O(E + V) space.

data.Brute-Force:
- Enumerate every subset of V-1 edges, keep those that are connected and acyclic, and pick the minimum total weight.
- This is exponential, roughly C(E, V-1) subsets.

data.Gotcha-Point: The accepted edges are the MST, so recording them at the point where you add to the weight sum gives the edge list for free. On a disconnected graph the V-1 break never fires, and you get a minimum spanning forest.

data.Optimal Approach:
- Use Prim's algorithm: a greedy approach that grows the MST from node 0.
- Keep a min-heap of {weight, node} holding the edges leaving the visited set.
- Pop the cheapest entry. If its node is already visited, skip it.
- Otherwise mark it visited, add its weight to the sum, and push the unvisited neighbours.
- Stop when the heap is empty, since the graph is connected.
- O(E log E) time, O(V + E) space.
